e: From Middle English losenge, from Old French losenge (“rhombus”), of uncertain origin.
q: Wherein the decussis is made within a longilaterall square, with opposite angles, acute and obtuse at the intersection; and so upon progression making a Rhombus or Lozenge figuration [...].
1658, Sir Thomas Browne, The Garden of Cyrus, Folio Society, published 2007, page 167:
How the junior partner of Hobbs and Dobbs leads her smiling to the carriage with the lozenge upon it, and the fat wheezy coachman!
1848, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 9, in Vanity Fair:
His sloppy socks were of scarlet wool with lilac lozenges; […]
1957 March 7, Vladimir Nabokov, chapter 1.1, in Pnin, Heinemann, page 7:
The floor is constructed from marble lozenges and triangles of every imaginable hue: yellow and pink and all manner of mottled and blotched shades, framed in white.
